I see how some people can watch flashy robot demos on the timeline and think with a shiver that the robot apocalypse is around the corner, but reality check: There is no robot in the world that can change the batteries in a jack-o-lantern. If you have a robot friendly door handle it might be able to walk outside, pick it up, and carry it back inside. The robot could open the drawer with your batteries in it, but then things get tough. Opening the package of AA batteries? Extracting a precision screwdriver from its case? Unscrewing four tiny screws that require a hard press and twist? Popping batteries out of the case? Yes, you could build and train a specialist robot to do that today, but there is a very long way to go to replace the full range of human capabilities. Near term doomer scenarios should stop at “secretly controlling humanity” instead of “wiping humanity out” 😀

RAG is so back! Another paper showing that plain RAG keeps winning the agent memory comparison. They show that many dedicated memory systems score below naive retrieval over the raw history on LongMemEval, PersonaMem, and MINT-Eval, while costing much more. They split a memory system's value into two parts. Memory benefit counts questions it answers that RAG misses. Memory tax counts questions RAG answers that the memory system gets wrong. Why does the tax appear? Building memory rewrites the history. Some facts get dropped or distorted during extraction, and some survive but become harder to retrieve. Memory systems also vary more than RAG when you change the backbone model. A simple fix helped. Retrieving from the raw history alongside memory and reranking both together reduced the tax. The practical takeaway here is that before adding a memory layer to your agent, compare it with plain retrieval over the transcript on your own data. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34073 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/memory-tax-dissecting-the-net-value-of-agent-memory-2610.34073

"We saw a glimpse of the future of swarm coding." Agent swarms will fundamentally change how we build software. @axiommathai used a swarm of agents to formally verify the Classification of Finite Simple Groups, the largest proof in math history. That is roughly 15,000 pages by over 100 mathematicians, now about 50 million lines of Lean, verified in 24 days. The agents claimed tasks, wrote proofs, reviewed each other, and merged their own work through GitHub. Along the way, they fixed hundreds of major errata in the published proof. The largest math proof in human history is now computer-verified. In the summer of 1994, a 23-year-old Elon Musk spent his days in Los Gatos at Pinnacle Research Institute, dreaming up how ultracapacitors could power electric cars and even Star Wars–style laser guns. Then, around 5 p.m. every evening, he drove to Palo Alto for his second job at Rocket Science Games, a startup full of future legends, from Tony Fadell, who would later build the iPod, to the people behind Apple's QuickTime and engineers from Industrial Light & Magic. They hired him to write the most boring code imaginable, drivers so joysticks and mice would work with games, but Elon quietly gave himself a much harder problem 😂: figuring out how a computer could run a game and stream video from a CD at the same time, something the machines of that era simply couldn't do. Peter Barrett, one of the company's founders, remembered him as "completely unflappable," and said that after a while nobody was giving him directions at all, because he was just building what he wanted to build. Bruce Leak, who hired him, said: "He had boundless energy." So yeah, nobody handed Elon the big problem, he just went looking for it, at night, after a full day at another job. Must-read paper from Microsoft Research and Georgia Tech. This one has lots of great insights. They used 163,487 Reddit posts about AI agents and surveyed 73 experienced agent users to map how delegated agent work goes wrong. The result is MANDATE, a taxonomy of 23 failure categories in seven groups. Each describes an agent that finishes the job in a way the user didn't expect. Users rated the most severe failures as the hardest to notice. People who had already run into a failure found it easier to spot than people who only thought it was possible. The most common failures are often the least studied. Agents that keep running and spend time and compute without making progress are among the most commonly reported failures, and they have the thinnest research base. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34748 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/babysitting-ai-agents-a-user-centered-taxonomy-and-study-of-agentic-delegation-f-2610.34748

An interesting idea on calibration of LLMs from @swyx when they were discussing Jev and decision models in @latentspacepod: > There’s one element of calibration which is a rare topic that I don’t think people even knew about or understood. We covered it with, our conversation with Clémentine Fourrier of Hugging Face, and she used to run the evals, at Hugging Face, which is basically the idea that, models are attuned to give you the most likely next token. But, they’re gonna lie to you when you ask them, “How confident are you?” Because they’re just gonna give you the most likely next answer instead of, like, actually, like, no, let’s calibrate. Like, I am actually fifty percent sure, or I am twenty percent sure, and, like, let’s try to calibrate that. I would say, like, if anything, I think that actually that’s pretty easy to generate synthetic data around because you can sort of see the truth and then synthetically generate a bunch of answers, have Jev classify it, and then compare with ground truth. That would be my reverse engineering of this. It was very nice to hear this because we've been exploring something very similar in our recent work on ProbabilityBench: creating synthetic data where we have access to the exact ground-truth probabilities to evaluate decision models and other LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17016 Calibration metrics are becoming popular for evaluating decision models, but they don't directly measure how close predicted probabilities are to the ground truth probabilities. A model can be perfectly calibrated while still producing inaccurate probability estimates for individual instances. So I also feel evaluating (and/or training) on synthetically generated data with ground truth probabilities might be a good way to go. Previously we had to rely on toy experiments with Gaussian distributions where we can analytically derive the ground truth probabilities (which is not suitable for testing LLMs), or had to use benchmarks with crude soft labels, e.g., CIFAR-10H, Fashion-MNIST-H, and ChaosNLI. Jev already uses synthetic data, and they may be doing something similar internally. While we don't know the details, some experiments shared in X suggest there's still room for improvement: when asked about a fair six-sided die, Jev assigned an average probability of ~83% to its chosen outcome (instead of 17%), and ~92% for a fair coin outcome (instead of 50%). This highlights how challenging getting accurate probabilities can be, even in these very simple settings. (see details in our blog: https://ishida-lab.github.io/blog_probabilitybench.html ) It would be exciting to see more research in this direction! Great paper from Alibaba and Cornell on verification in coding-agent harnesses. (bookmark it) If you build agent harnesses, this one is worth your time. They find that a separate reviewer agent adds 5.9 to 9.5 points on Terminal-Bench at 1.13 to 1.25x the baseline cost. They compared 17 verification designs across seven frontier coding models on Terminal-Bench and SWE-bench Verified. The designs check the agent's work at four points: the initial instructions, reminders during the run, a gate before the agent can finish, and an independent critic at the end. Instructions and reminders gave small, model-dependent gains. Completion gates gave larger gains, sometimes at much higher cost. The critic gave the best accuracy per dollar, adding 3.9 to 6.6 points on SWE-bench Verified at almost no extra cost. More review rounds added up to 3.5 more points on Terminal-Bench. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34577 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/rethinking-verification-in-agent-harnesses-2610.34577
